title: Using an Ecological Momentary Assessment (EMA) Smartphone Application in the Treatment of Binge Eating Disorder: A Proof-of-Concept Study
content: Objective: Cognitive behaviour therapy (CBT) for binge eating disorder (BED) is fairly effective, yet relapse remains problematic. Treatment outcomes may be improved if patients obtain more insight in symptom patterns. In this proof-of-concept study embedded in BED treatment, we evaluated the use of an Ecological Momentary Assessment (EMA) smartphone application to self-monitor affect and binge eating episodes in daily life. Methods: Participants were 20 adults who received group-CBT for BED at a mental health institute in the Netherlands. Via an EMA smartphone app, participants filled out 5 micro-questionnaires daily for 6 weeks. An overview of mood fluctuations and binge eating episodes was graphically displayed in the app and discussed with the therapist. Afterwards, semi-structured interviews were conducted with 16 participants and 5 practitioners to evaluate feasibility and usefulness. Results: Qualitative analyses of the interviews showed that the app was perceived as user-friendly, yet invasive due to many registrations. This was reflected in low response rates (mean: 31.1%), with only 9 participants reaching a response rate above 30% (>65 of 210 EMA micro-questionnaires completed). Some participants thought the daily registrations were insightful, but some also perceived the registrations as confronting and shameful. Conclusions: This study offers a real-world example of using EMA in treatment and provides meaningful insights for developers of behaviour change-focused EMA tools. The experiences of participants and practitioners were mixed, yet for several, awareness in (fluctuations in) emotions seemed to improve. For BED treatment, EMA may be best implemented during a short period of time as add-on tool to personalize treatment rather than as a one-size-fits-all approach.
